title: A 2,200-Year-Old Ship's Sticky Secret
summary:
A Roman ship that sank about 2,200 years ago near Croatia is telling us how people long ago kept their ships safe from the sea. Scientists found two kinds of waterproof coating on the ship. One was made of pine tar. The other was pine tar mixed with beeswax.

People who build ships have always had the same problem: how to keep water out and protect wood from salt water, tiny living things, and sea animals called shipworms.

In a new study, scientists from France and Croatia looked at the coatings of a ship called Ilovik-Parzine 1. The ship sank about 2,200 years ago, when Rome was a republic. The scientists found two kinds of coating. One was pine tar, also called pitch. The other was pine tar mixed with beeswax. Greek shipbuilders called that mix zopissa.

The beeswax made the coating bendy and easy to spread when hot. That helped a lot on wooden ships, because wood moves and bends in waves.
why_it_matters: It shows how clever people long ago were at solving everyday problems with things from nature.
